blocks.heading: Markets and marketing
blocks.text: A market brings buyers and sellers into contact for exchange of a particular good or service; it need not be a physical place. Marketing is the management process which identifies consumer wants and anticipates their future wants. It guides decisions about how an offering meets those wants through product, price, promotion and distribution. Research collects information and advertising communicates promotional messages; both can contribute to the wider marketing role but neither is its complete definition. Good marketing connects understanding customers with a feasible offering, rather than merely persuading people to buy whatever has already been made.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nera Bags interviews potential buyers, adjusts bag capacity, chooses a price and arranges where the bags can be bought. The interviews are research within a wider marketing process. Decisions about the offering and access show why marketing is broader than an advertisement.

blocks.heading: A market
blocks.text: A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a particular product or service. Contact can occur at a stall, through a shop, by telephone or online. Define what is being traded and the relevant buyers or area when comparing markets. A market is not the activity of marketing or merely the physical building where sales occur.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Oru Repairs accepts bookings through phone calls and completes repairs at customers’ homes. There is still a market for its repair service even without customers meeting at a market stall.

blocks.heading: Marketing
blocks.text: Marketing is the management process which identifies consumer wants and anticipates their future wants. It supports decisions about the offering and how customers obtain it, not simply promotional communication. Research is one information-gathering activity within it. A business needs to connect identified wants with realistic product, price, promotion and access choices.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nalu Meals investigates preferences and adapts its meal and collection arrangements. The customer-focused process is marketing; a poster announcing collection times is only one promotional element.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why Tano Meals’ customer survey and poster are not complete definitions of marketing.

The survey is market research, collecting information; the poster is advertising, communicating a promotional message. Marketing is the wider process identifying and anticipating wants and guiding how an offering meets them. Product, price and access decisions remain beyond those two activities.
